1 Problem Definition

1.1 Insight into cirrhosis

Cirrhosis is a condition that occurs when a person’s liver undergoes severe long term damage, and its main consequence for a patient is the formation of scar tissue on the liver, called fibrosis, taking over healthy liver tissue (Ilyas, 2026). It can be described as the “terminal histopathological stage of diverse chronic liver conditions”, and some of its main causes include various types of hepatitis and excessive alcohol consumption (Luo et al., 2025). This terminal condition requires a liver transplant because scarring of the tissue is permanent, but if its not caught early in patients or left untreated it can lead to death. In 2017, cirrhosis was the cause of 2.4% of global deaths (increased rate from previous years), with higher statistics in certain regions, like North Africa and Middle East (Luo et al., 2025). Looking into factors which can potentially increase chances of mortality in cirrhosis patients, presence of ascities is hypothesized to increase chances of death. Ascites is the abnormal buildup of excess fluid inside the peritoneal cavity (“Ascites”, 2025). Cirrhosis occurs in 2 stages, the compensated and the decompensated stage, the latter having a median survival time of approximately 2 years, compared to the first stage’s survival time of more than 12 years, with the decompensanted stage associated with the presence of ascities (D’Amico et al., 2006). It is therefore logical that ascities can correspond to a higher chance of death. Furthermore, many papers investigating cirrhosis cite the Child-Pugh score as a reliable predictor of chance of death of cirrhosis patients, some of its components are bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin, and ascities (D’Amico et al., 2006). All of these metrics above of a patient are investigated in this research, so it is hypothesized that they will have a positive increase in chance of death of patients. The extent to which they increase chances of death from a 1 unit increase in them is also investigated. Research into factors that contribute, or hint at, a higher risk of mortality from cirrhosis is important because it can provide insight into which patients are at a greater risk and should be considered for liver transplants earlier. It can also improve detection strategies and provide medical professionals with information on how treatment can be enhanced to limit mortality. Cirrhosis patients can benefit from this research as it could provide more clarity about the risks of their illness, and certainty into when action should be taken.

1.2 Methodology

The main objective of this research is to develop a model with examines which medical metrics are associated with a higher patient mortality from cirrhosis.

Research question: Which medical metrics can indicate a higher chance of death for a patient with cirrhosis, and to what extent do they contribute to the chance of mortality? Can a predictive model be built for patient survival prediction?

The research question will be investigated using a supervised machine learning analytical approach, examining medical records of patients with cirrhosis (the inputs) with a known survival outcome. The survival outcome of a patient is the target variable. In the unedited data set its a factor variable with 3 levels: deceased, received a liver transplant, and alive at the time of the end of data collection. Individual patients with cirrhosis are the units of observation in this research. Models like the Naive Bayes, K - Nearest Neighbor algorithm, logistic regression analysis, and a stepwise regression model will be used to create insight on the relationship between input variables and the target variable, and possibly offer some predictive capabilities for patient mortality.

1.3 Packages used

For this research, the following R packages are utilised:

  • liver: Used for data partitioning.
  • naivebayes: Used for creating a Naive Bayes model.
  • ggplot2: Used for graphs and data visualization.
  • pROC: Used for model evaluation using ROC curves.
  • psych: Used for the pairs.panels() function.
  • Metrics: Used for the mse function.
  • readr: Used for importing the data into R.
  • Hmisc: Used for imputation of missing values.
  • ggcorrplot: Used for creating correlation matrices between numerical variables.
  • naniar: Used to check for missing observations

To load the R packages:

library(liver)           
library(naivebayes)
library(ggplot2)
library(pROC)          
library(psych) 
library(Metrics) 
library(readr)
library(Hmisc)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(naniar)

2 Data Acquisition

The data set used in this research is from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository, stemming from a study conducted between 1974 and 1984 by the Mayo Clinic on primary biliary cirrhosis patients that were at the clinic for treatment (Dickson et al., 1989). The patient’s medical information was collected from participants of a randomized trial of the D-penicillamine drug as a possible treatment for cirrhosis, and patients who were at the clinic for treatment but did not participate in the trial. The study included 312 patients who participated in the study, amongst whom around half (158) were administered the D-penicillamine drug and a control group of 154 who were given a placebo, the 112 patients who did not participate in the trial also consented to data collection, and 6 of the those patients had stopped contact with the clinic after their diagnosis (Dickson et al., 1989). The data that was collected from the patients includes information on their survival (or whether they received a liver transplant) and their collected medical metrics, such as components in their blood and physical features of their livers. The observational units represented by rows of the data set are individual patients who participated in the data collection process, each having their own unique ID (1st column). The data also has some basic information on patients, like their age and gender. Please refer to the Data Understanding and Exploration section for an overview of all the variables present in the data set. The original format of the data is a CSV file, and it was accessed through a open source data repository. The license of this data set is Creative Commons BY 4.0, meaning that it is allowed to be used for any purpose with proper crediting. The patients are not listed by any identifiable characteristics, so their anonymity is preserved.

Firstly, loading the cirrhosis data set as a .csv file as “data” for the analysis.

data <- read_csv("cirrhosis.csv")

The output of the str function is a spec tibble dataframe object spc_tbl_df. This object class is from the readr package. Essentially, this is just a table with column specific data. This gives an overview of all 20 variables from the cirrhosis.csv dataset:

  • ID*: Categorical (nominal), a unique identifier for each observation (patient), expressed as a number.

  • N_days: Numerical (count), number of days between registration and the earlier of death, transplantation or study analysis time in July 1986.**

  • Status: Categorical (nominal), status of the patient C (censored), CL (censored due to liver transplant), or D (death). The C and CL categories effectively also mean that the patient survived treatment until the end of data collection.

  • Drug: Categorical (binary), type of drug administered to patient: D-penicillamine or placebo

  • Age: Numerical (count), age of patient in days

  • Sex: Categorical (binary), sex of the patient, M (Male) or F (female)

  • Ascites: Categorical (binary), presence of ascites, abnormal buildup of excess fluid inside the peritoneal cavity (“Ascites”, 2025), N (No) or Y (Yes)

  • Hepatomegaly: Categorical (binary), presence of hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), N (No) or Y (Yes)

  • Spiders: Categorical (binary), presence of spiders (swollen blood vessels), N (No) or Y (Yes)

  • Edema: Categorical (nominal), presence of edema N (no edema and no diuretic therapy for edema), S (edema present without diuretics, or edema resolved by diuretics), Y (edema present despite diuretic therapy)

  • Bilirubin: Numerical (continuous), serum bilirubin in blood, measured in mg/dl

  • Cholesterol: Numerical (continuous), serum cholesterol in blood, measured in mg/dl

  • Albumin: Numerical (continuous), albumin in blood, measured in gm/dl

  • Copper: Numerical (continuous), copper in urine, measured in ug/day

  • Alk_Phos: Numerical (continuous), alkaline phosphatase levels in blood, measured in U/l

  • SGOT: Numerical (continuous), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase levels in blood, measured in U/ml

  • Triglycerides: Numerical (continuous), triglycerides in blood, measured in mg/dl

  • Platelets: Numerical (continuous), platelets in blood, measured per cubic ml/1000

  • Prothrombin: Numerical (continuous), prothrombin time, measured in seconds

  • Stage: Categorical (ordinal), histologic stage of the disease, (1, 2, 3, or 4)

  • Important to note - this variable is not based on any real patient characteristics, and hence will be excluded from any analysis. ** This variable’s values are based on the outcome of the patient, the variable Status. Therefore, this variable leads to data leakage and should be removed, as this is only known after the outcome and is dependent on the outcome. Therefore, we will exclude the variable N_Days from our analysis.

3.2 Exploring the target variable

The target variable is status, which indicates whether a patient died during treatment (D), survived (C) or had their status censored due to a liver transplant (CL), as the cirrhosis affected tissue was removed and hence the patient did not die due to cirrhosis, but the patient’s improved condition was not due to the treatment.

The target variable status is examined using geom_bar function from ggplot2 to create a bar plot to visualize the target variable.

ggplot(data = data) + 
    geom_bar(aes(x = Status), fill = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) +
    labs(title = "Bar plot for the target variable 'status'")

Here, the summary function is used to create a table of the target variable so the exact number of observations for each category is visible.

data$Status <- as.factor(data$Status)
summary(data$Status)
    C  CL   D 
  232  25 161

It is apparent that for both, dead and censored categories, there is a sufficiently large sample size for analysis and modeling. The Censored due to liver transplant category is not large enough, however, therefore it will be combined with the censored category, to create a binary variable of called survived with the categories “Yes” and “No”. Although one can not confidently state that a patient who is in the censored category survived, the category does state that the patient did not die at the clinic during treatment due to cirrhosis. It is also important to note that those who had a liver transplant did not survive cirrhosis or have their condition improve due to treatment.

3.3 Exploration of predictors

Missing observations

Firstly, all variables are checked for missing observations. This is done with the naniar package.

gg_miss_var(data, show_pct = TRUE )

There is a significant number of missing values across many variables in the data set. Missing values for Drug and the rest of the variables are dealt with separately in Data preparation for modeling. Refer to the section after the boxplot for Drug to see exactly how its missing values are dealt with. Missing values for other variables will be imputed separately after data partitioning.

Drug

A key variable is the “Drug” variable, as this was part of the Mayo Clinic’s trial to see whether D-penicillamine could be used as an effective treatment for acute cirrhosis. Therefore, the drug variable is investigated in depth.

table(data$Drug)
  
  D-penicillamine         Placebo 
              158             154
table(data$Status, data$Drug, dnn = c("Status", "Drug"))
        Drug
  Status D-penicillamine Placebo
      C               83      85
      CL              10       9
      D               65      60
ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Drug, fill = Status)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) # this allows us to see the absolute counts for each category of the drug variable

ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Drug, fill = Status), position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) +
  labs(y = "Proportion", x = "Drug", fill = "Status") # the position = "fill" argument let's use visually intuitively compare the proportions of each category of status for the drug variable

Judging by pure volume, the category of patients who did not participate in the drug trial has fewer deaths than those who did. However, looking at proportion, patients who were administered the placebo have a slightly lower death proportion compared to the D-penicillamine intake patients. There is not a large discrepancy in the proportions across the 3 categories, so this relationship may prove to be insignificant. There is a significant proportion of the sample population who have a missing value of NA for the Drug variable. This is key to note for the data preparation step, as these observations should be dropped. This is because these values are missing as the patients under the NA category for Drug did not participate in the drug trial, and hence were also not administered the D-penicillamine nor a placebo. It would be data fabrication to have their values imputed and hence these observations should be dropped, even though they represent a significant portion of the data set. After removing these observations, there should still be over 300 observations, still enough to conduct data analysis using Naive Bayes and kNN algorithms.

Stage of the disease

There is a clear association between the stage of the disease and the patient’s status. Although stage 1 does not have a large enough sample size, hence it should be added to stage 2 to create a combined category for the lower 2 stages. Nevertheless, its apparent from the graph how patients in stage 4 are much less likely to survive. However, it should also be noted that this is likely a confounding variable, as if the disease has progressed further, it logically follows it is more likely to be fatal, as it was outlined in the introduction.

ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Stage, fill = Status)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) # allows us to see the absolute counts of the Stage variable

ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Stage, fill = Status), position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) +
  labs(y = "Proportion", x = "Stage", fill = "Status") # allows us to see the proportions of the status variable for each category of the Stage variable

Sex

ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Sex, fill = Status)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) # creates a bar chart for the absolute counts of the sex variable

ggplot(data = data) + 
  geom_bar(aes(x = Sex, fill = Status), position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48"))  + 
  labs(y = "Proportion", x = "Sex", fill = "Status")

# creates a bar chart which allows us to see proportions of the Status variable for each category of the sex variable

There is a significant discrepancy between the sexes, as was expected, as cirrhosis is more commonly present in women at a 9-to-1 ratio. This data set has almost 50 male patients and over 400 female patients, which would actually be an over representation of men relative to the expected ratio. Consequently, however, the low number of male patients also means that the results for this variable are more susceptible to noise, and are hence less reliable. Any analysis based on the relationship of the sex variable to the status variable should consider the imbalance. Looking at the proportions, male cirrhosis patients have a higher death rate than female patients.

Age

ggplot(data, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 365, fill = "#fbc531", color = "#353b48") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Age", x = "Age", y = "Count")

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Status, y = Age), fill = c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48")) 

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_density(aes(x = Age, fill = Status, color = Status), alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#e84118", "#353b48")) +
  scale_color_manual(values =c("#fbc531", "#e1b12c", "#353b48"))

Comparing the box plots for age, the median, 1st quartile and 3rd quartile are all somewhat higher for dead patients and their age compared to the patients whose status was censored. This suggests that age could be a factor increasing the likelihood of death. It appears that patients who received a liver transplant were also, on average, younger. Also of note is that age is expressed in the number of days a person has been alive. Although this helps for precision, it makes interpreting the data unintuitive, and hence age will be recoded to reflect a patient’s age in years.

Numerical variables

In order to investigate numerical variables, a correlation plot is used to check for confounding variables and collinearity.

variableslist2 = c("Age", "N_Days", "Bilirubin", "Cholesterol", "Albumin", "Copper", "Alk_Phos", "SGOT", "Tryglicerides", "Platelets", "Prothrombin")

cor_matrix <- cor(data[, variableslist2], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

ggcorrplot(cor_matrix, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 4, colors = c("#353b48", "white", "#e1b12c"))

Bilirubin has some medium correlations with some other variables, which are stronger than most other correlations between other variables. This graph shows that these variables for the most are mostly weakly correlated with each other, however very few have a correlation of 0 or very close to 0. In general, there are no strong or clear correlations between variables nor confounding variables, therefore, according the the correlation matrix, there is no reason to remove any of the variables from the data set. Aside from the N_Days variable which is removed due to it stemming from status.

Please see the Data preparation for modeling section on further visual analysis of non-target variables. This was done because recoding the target variable to combine the 2 censored categories into 1 offers more insightful exploration of variables, since the outcome of this research is to investigate death vs. survival.

4 Data preparation for modeling

It is important to note that dropping missing observations from the drug variable, recoding age, and combining categories of status is done before data partitioning. Status is recoded beforehand to match the scope of the research question and define it as a binary variable. Age is recoded for purely interpretative reasons, it is not reliant on the data and other observations. Dropping missing observations for Drug is also done beforehand because this is not a data reliant decision, only concerning the scope of the research.

4.1 Recoding variables

The first step in data preparation is to combine the categories of censored and censored due to liver transplant. This is done because the analysis focuses on chances of patient death, and patients who got a liver transplant did not, potentially, die from cirrhosis, so the only logical categories to combine is alive and got a liver transplant.

This is done with the following code:

data$Survived <- ifelse(data$Status != "D", "Yes", "No") 

data$Survived <- factor(data$Survived, levels = c("Yes", "No"))

A double-check is done on the new Survived variable.

table(data$Status) # table for the Status variable
  
    C  CL   D 
  232  25 161
table(data$Survived) # table for the new, recoded version of the Status variable "Survived"
  
  Yes  No 
  257 161

Comparing it to the old table for Status, the yes category is the sum of the C and CL categories, while no, meaning patients who passed away, has remained the same as the category D for the Status variable.

The variable Age is also recoded, as it is currently unintuitive to interpret, as it displays its values in days. It is recoded into years by dividing it by 365.25, as this gives the closest value in years to the true age of the patient.

data$age_year <- data$Age/365.25

Taking a step back to data exploration, this binary variable is used to explore other variables using boxplots. The boxplots can be compared on how they differ between the patients who survived and those who did not for each variable.

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = Survived, fill = Survived)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#353b48")) +
  labs(title = "Bar plot for the target binary variable 'Survived'")

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = age_year), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48")) 

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Cholesterol), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Albumin), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Copper), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Alk_Phos), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = SGOT), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Tryglicerides), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Platelets), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Prothrombin), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48")) 

ggplot(data = data) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Survived, y = Stage), fill = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"))

Some variables visually indicate a higher mortality rate among larger observation of predictor variables by having quartiles and/or median values be higher for the No category of survived. That includes: prothrombin, tryglicerides, SGOT, Alk_Phos, copper, and cholesterol. This aligns with the hypothesis regarding the Child-Pugh score, that higher metrics of its components lead to an increased chance of death. Some variables indicate the opposite relationship, lower counts of predictor variable are linked to less deaths. That includes platelets and albumin. Something to note from some of the boxplots, is that there are many variables which have outliers, for example Copper. They will not be removed, as they represent true measures of a medical indicator. Even though they are rare and outliers when compared to most patients, they still are realistic results for such tests, especially for patients with acute cirrhosis. Additionally, there are no outliers of 0, which would be the only impossible case for medical metrics.

4.2 Missing values

As mentioned, the drug variable includes a significant number of missing values and this data can not be imputed, as the missing value represents patients who did not participate in the drug trial, as we are interested in finding out whether the drug D-penicillamine is an effective treatment and whether it has an effect on patient survival, the rows with a missing value need to be dropped in the drug category.

data_noNA <- data[!is.na(data$Drug), ]

Using summary to check if the rows were correctly dropped, it is visible that the length of many features is now 312, indicating that the missing values for the variable Drug have been removed and the appropriate rows dropped across all variables. Despite this, more missing values are still present across our data. However, these values will be imputed, as these missing values reflect a real value for each patient and are missing at random. Imputation will be done after the data has been partitioned into a test and training set.

4.3 Data partitioning

In order to avoid data leakage, there is a need to partition the data into a test and training set. The training set will be used to create models, which will be used on the test set. It is important that any data imputation and parameters based on the data and set for the models are based on only the training data, to avoid overly optimistic estimates of model performance. As there is a little over 300 observations, the partition will be made with 33% for the test set and 67% for the training set, to ensure that the test set has at least 100 observations. Stratification is not needed since the target variable is well represented across both of its levels.

The set.seed() function is used to ensure replicability of the study, as using the same seed would produce the same results even on another computer.

set.seed(26)
split_data = partition(data = data_noNA, ratio = c(0.67, 0.33))

data_train = split_data$part1 # we assign the larger partition to the training set
data_test = split_data$part2 # we assign the smaller partition to the test set

data_true_test = data_test$Survived # for ease of access, create a variable specifically for the Survived variable of the test set
test_labels = data_test$Survived
summary(data_true_test)
  Yes  No 
   60  43
summary(data_train$Survived)
  Yes  No 
  127  82
summary(data_noNA$Survived)
  Yes  No 
  187 125

The partition is deemed valid if the proportions of the target variable are similar across the training and the test set.

60/(60+43) # the proportion of the target variable Survived for the test set
  [1] 0.5825243
127/(127+83) # the proportion of the target variable Survived for the training set
  [1] 0.6047619
187/(187+125) # the proportion of the target variable Survived for the entire cirrhosis dataset
  [1] 0.599359

The proportions are all quite similar, with the small differences due to using a count and the relatively low overall number of observations of the cirrhosis data set. However, the differences are minimal and hence the partition has been validated.

Looking at the summary for the training set, there are still some variables with missing values. However, for these cases, one can not assume that the missing value is structural. In reality, these patients still had a valid value for each variable, it just was not recorded due to incidental reasons. The value does exist in reality, it simply was not recorded in this data set. Therefore, the value is imputed based on the existing values in the training set. The impute function from the Hmisc package is used to impute the missing values. First, however, an _observed object is created for each variable from the real recorded observations in the training set, which will be used later for imputation of missing values for the test set. The object is created for each variable, as it is possible the test set has missing values, even if the training set does not. To make sure the test set has no missing values, we therefore need to store the observed values of each variable based on the training set.

# create an object for each variable which takes the real observed values from the training set
chol_observed <- data_train$Cholesterol[!is.na(data_train$Cholesterol)]
copper_observed <- data_train$Copper[!is.na(data_train$Copper)]
Alk_Phos_observed <- data_train$Alk_Phos[!is.na(data_train$Alk_Phos)]
sgot_observed <- data_train$SGOT[!is.na(data_train$SGOT)]
trig_observed <- data_train$Tryglicerides[!is.na(data_train$Tryglicerides)]
platelets_observed <- data_train$Platelets[!is.na(data_train$Platelets)]
prot_observed <- data_train$Prothrombin[!is.na(data_train$Prothrombin)]
spiders_observed <- data_train$Spiders[!is.na(data_train$Spiders)]
ascites_observed <- data_train$Ascites[!is.na(data_train$Ascites)]
hepatomegaly_observed <- data_train$Hepatomegaly[!is.na(data_train$Hepatomegaly)]
stage_observed <- data_train$Stage[!is.na(data_train$Stage)]

# impute missing values based on each variables own parameters for the training set. 
# Using the "random" setting the impute function randomly selects a value from the observed values of
# the training set and inserts the random value back into the variable

data_train$Ascites = impute(data_train$Ascites, fun = "random")

data_train$Hepatomegaly = impute(data_train$Hepatomegaly, fun = "random")

data_train$Spiders = impute(data_train$Spiders, fun = "random")

data_train$Cholesterol = impute(data_train$Cholesterol, fun = "random")

data_train$Copper = impute(data_train$Copper, fun = "random")

data_train$Alk_Phos = impute(data_train$Alk_Phos, fun = "random")

data_train$SGOT = impute(data_train$SGOT, fun = "random")

data_train$Tryglicerides = impute(data_train$Tryglicerides, fun = "random")


data_train$Platelets = impute(data_train$Platelets, fun = "random")

data_train$Prothrombin = impute(data_train$Prothrombin, fun = "random")

data_train$Stage = impute(data_train$Stage, fun = "random")

data_train_prep = droplevels(data_train) # this removes unused value labels. Value categories with no entries would create issues for algorithms such as Naive Bayes

The training set is now prepared, with no missing values. To impute the missing values in the test set, the observed values from the training data are used. Directly imputing the test set would leak information from the test set into the analysis and hence cause data leakage. Instead, before imputing the training set, the observed training values of each variable were stored. A for loop is used to go through the variables and replace each missing test value with a value randomly sampled from the corresponding training values. This way, the test set is imputed using only information from the training set.

# we create a list of variables to use in the for loop

vars_to_fill <- list(
  Copper = copper_observed,
  Alk_Phos = Alk_Phos_observed,
  SGOT = sgot_observed,
  Tryglicerides = trig_observed,
  Platelets = platelets_observed,
  Cholesterol = chol_observed,
  Prothrombin = prot_observed,
  Spiders = spiders_observed,
  Ascites = ascites_observed,
  Hepatomegaly = hepatomegaly_observed,
  Stage = stage_observed
)

# here we use a for loop to replace all missing values in the test set based on the observed values of the training set

for (var in names(vars_to_fill)) {
  na_idx <- is.na(data_test[[var]])
  data_test[[var]][na_idx] <- sample(vars_to_fill[[var]], size = sum(na_idx), replace = TRUE)
}
data_test_prep = droplevels(data_test)

Now the data set is prepared with no missing values.

However, an issue that was discovered from the summaries of the training and test set, is that the Stage variable is currently computed as a numerical variable. It is to be recoded into a categorical variable, as it should be. Additionally, the lower 2 stages (stage 1 and 2) are combined into a single category since stage 1 has a small number of observations. The variable then will have 3 levels, 1 3 and 4, where 1 represents stages 1 and 2, 3 represents stage 3, and 4 represents stage 4.

data_train_prep$Stage = as.character(data_train_prep$Stage)
data_train_prep$Stage[data_train_prep$Stage %in% c("1", "2")] = "1"
data_train_prep$Stage = factor(data_train_prep$Stage, levels = c("1", "3", "4"))

data_test_prep$Stage = as.character(data_test_prep$Stage)
data_test_prep$Stage[data_test_prep$Stage %in% c("1", "2")] = "1"
data_test_prep$Stage = factor(data_test_prep$Stage, levels = levels(data_train_prep$Stage)) # this applies the same levels of the training set for the test set
table(data_train_prep$Stage, data_train_prep$Survived)
     
      Yes No
    1  47 11
    3  51 25
    4  29 46

Now the Stage variable is a categorical variable and we have prepared the data for modeling.

5 Modeling

First, based on the exploratory analysis, an object predictors is created which act as the formula in the analysis. In the formula, all variables which are included in the data set are used, except for ID, as this is not a variable related to the patient’s condition. N_days is also not included for reasons outlined earlier.

predictors <- Survived ~ Drug + age_year + Sex + Ascites + Hepatomegaly + Spiders + Edema + Bilirubin + Cholesterol + Albumin + Copper + Alk_Phos + SGOT + Tryglicerides + Platelets + Prothrombin + Stage

A logistic regression, Naive Bayes and k nearest neighbour (kNN) algorithms are used and models for each of them respectively will be created. Logistic regression is a standard modeling method used when the target variable is a binary variable, as is the case with this data and it allows for straightforward interpretability for all predictors in the data set using odds ratios. Naive Bayes is a model which works well when dealing with multiple variable types, as is the case in this data set, as it includes both categorical and numerical data. Naive Bayes also works well in data sets with lower number of observations, as is also the case with this data set, as the data after dropping missing values from the Drug variable has 312 observations remaining in total. Naive Bayes, however, works under the assumptions that all data and all events are independent, which is not the case with this dataset, nor in many other real life scenarios. That being said, it’s efficiency, ease of use and low variable requirement makes it useful in a practical setting. kNN model will also be used, as it makes no assumption about the shape of the relationship and can effectively capture non-linear relationships. However, kNN requires some additional data preparation, due to being sensitive to the scale of values and requiring dummy encoding of categorical values as it measures the Euclidean distance between observations in its algorithm. The models are supplemented with a stepwise regression model, which is used to find which variables are the most relevant for practical use and to remove variables from the models which exhibit collinearity or which do not give enough new information for the model to be of practical use. A comparison will be made with the full set of variables and the reduced set of variables found by the stepwise regression model for all models and evaluating their performance respectively. The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is used as a measure for how much a variable adds to the model. AIC penalizes model complexity, and hence prefers simpler models with less variables. Additionally, all of the models mentioned are suitable for a classification task for a binary variable.

For model evaluation and to set a benchmark for the models, a model which always predicts “Yes” as the baseline is used, because “Yes” is the more common category for the target variable Survived.

summary(data_true_test)
  Yes  No 
   60  43

5.1 Logistic and stepwise regression

A logistic regression was chosen as one of the models. Firstly, a binomial family model is used with the No category of the Survived target variable as a reference category. This means that the odds ratios provided by the model reflect the chances of a patient passing away from cirrhosis, and it can be compared to the survival odds. Furthermore, this classification method can be compared with kNN and Naive Bayes models to judge model performance. For the first regression, all variables are used as predictive variables, and it is adjusted using a step wise method.

levels(data_train_prep$Survived)
  [1] "Yes" "No"
logreg_all = glm(predictors, data = data_train_prep, family = binomial) # binomial family models the "No" category, therefore the odds ratios reflect the odds of the "No" category compared to the "Yes" category for the target variable, meaning odds of death

# Calculate the odds ratios

At a significance level of 5%, the variables age, alkaline phosphatase, SGOT, and prothrombin are significant. Below are interpretations of their impact on survival for each one, holding all the other variables constant. A 1 year increase in age is associated with an increase in odds of death by 5.69%. A 1 unit increase in alkaline phosphatase is associated with an increase in odds of death by 0.0248%. A 1 unit increase in SGOT is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 1.0013%. A 1 unit increase in prothrombin is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 55.85%.

These variables showed a visual difference in the survival variable in the data exploration step, therefore, the relationship is as hypothesized. However, many of these variables might overlap due to collinearity. Therefore a stepwise regression is run on the training set to determine if any of the predictor variables can be removed from the logistic regression.

predictors_new = Survived ~ age_year + Ascites + Bilirubin + Copper + Alk_Phos + SGOT + Platelets + Prothrombin

Following from the stepwise regression model, 9 of the 17 variables used in the formula predictors are removed. Using the AIC criterion, the variables Drug, Sex, Hepatomegaly, Spiders, Edema, Cholesterol, Albumin, Stage and Triglycerides are deemed as not contributing enough additional information to be retained and hence complicate the model unnecessarily. This is shown by the AIC decreasing from 205.27 to 190.27 in the step wise process, indicating that the new combination of predictors is better suited for the logistic regression. The variables that are significant at a 5% level are age, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, SGOT, platelets, and prothrombin. The stepwise model has more significant predictor variable coefficients than the full model. Additionally, one of the coefficients appears to have a negative effect on chances of death of a patient, that is platelets. It is worth noting that the variables have different standard quantities in the blood/urine of a person, and a 1 unit increase can be large for some variables but small for others. Below are the interpretations of each one of the coefficients, holding all the other variables constant:

A 1 year increase in age is associated with an increase in odds of death by 5.68%. Age is also significant at a 1% level. A 1 unit increase in bilirubin is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 22.056%. A 1 unit increase in alkaline phosphatase is associated with an increase in odds of death by 0.0245%. A 1 unit increase in SGOT is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 1.0070%. A 1 unit increase in platelets is associated with a decrease in odds of death of a patient by 0.47197%. A 1 unit increase in prothrombin is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 54.2541%.

5.2 kNN

For the kNN algorithm, one additional step of data preparation is completed, the categorical variables need dummy encoding, as the kNN algorithm calculates euclidean distances between values. A categorical variable does not have a numerical value which can be used for calculating euclidean distance, therefore any categorical variables are encoded into binary variables, where the binary nature is used to calculate distance. Each category will be turned into a dummy variable of its own. The data set has two categorical variables - Edema and Stage. A copy of the training and test sets are used to eliminate the chance that dummy variables will interfere with other models. A kNN algorithm was chosen because it can be used to classify a patient into a binary outcome, and it does not assume that the relationship between predictors is strictly linear, like a regression does. Therefore, it can provide useful insights beyond that.

train_set_kNN = as.data.frame(data_train_prep) # we create a copy of training and test set for the kNN algorithm, as we do not want dummy variables to be present during other analysis
test_set_kNN = as.data.frame(data_test_prep)


train_set_kNN$Edema <- as.factor(data_train_prep$Edema)
test_set_kNN$Edema  <- as.factor(data_test_prep$Edema)

summary(test_set_kNN$Edema)

categorical_features = c("Edema", "Stage")

train_onehot = one.hot(train_set_kNN, cols = categorical_features)
test_onehot  = one.hot(test_set_kNN,  cols = categorical_features)

Before a kNN algorithm is run on the dataset, the best value of k is found based on the training set by examining model accuracy with different k values. Here another key data preparation step for the kNN algorithm is done. The function kNN has a “scaler” argument. Minmax scaling is used, which automatically transforms all numerical variables into a scale of 0-1 for the kNN algorithm, as it uses the Euclidean distance formula in its algorithm for determining the distance between each observation and hence the nearest neighbours based on that distance. This is important, as some variables, for example Alk_Phos, can often go into 4-digit values, whereas a variable such as Bilirubin has much lower values. Without scaling, the Alk_Phos variable would have a much greater influence on the distance result of the Euclidean distance formula. Minmax scaling scales everything to a uniform scale, by placing the value of every observations on a scale of 0-1, where 1 is the highest value for the relevant variable and 0 the lowest.

predictors_knn = Survived ~ Drug + age_year + Sex + Ascites + Hepatomegaly + Spiders + Edema_N + Edema_S + Edema_Y + Bilirubin + Cholesterol + Albumin + Copper + Alk_Phos + SGOT + Tryglicerides + Platelets + Prothrombin + Stage_1 + Stage_3 + Stage_4
# the kNN.plot function allows us to compare the accuracy of different values of k for the kNN algorithm. We use the minmax scaler, for our kNN analysis, which transforms all variables automatically to a scale of 0-1.
kNN.plot(predictors_knn, train = train_onehot, ratio = c(0.67, 0.33), scaler = "minmax", 
          k.max = 30, set.seed = 26)
  Setting levels: reference = "Yes", case = "No"

And also for the reduced set of predictors.

kNN.plot(predictors_new, train = train_onehot, ratio = c(0.67, 0.33), scaler = "minmax", 
          k.max = 30, set.seed = 26)
  Setting levels: reference = "Yes", case = "No"

From these plots it can concluded that the accuracy of the kNN model is highest when the value of k = 5 for the model using all predictors, and k = 9 for the model with the reduced set of predictors.

# here we create kNN probability vectors for the full set of predictors. 

kNN_5_all = kNN(predictors_knn, train = train_onehot, test = test_onehot, scaler = "minmax", k = 5)

prob_kNN_all = kNN(
  predictors_knn,
  train = train_onehot,
  test = test_onehot,
  scaler = "minmax",
  k = 5,
  type = "prob"
)

# here we create kNN probability vectors for the new, reduced set of predictors
kNN_9_new = kNN(predictors_new, train = train_onehot, test = test_onehot, scaler = "minmax", k = 9)

prob_kNN_new = kNN(
  predictors_new,
  train = train_onehot,
  test = test_onehot,
  scaler = "minmax",
  k = 9,
  type = "prob"
)
summary(kNN_5_all)
  Yes  No 
   74  29
summary(kNN_9_new)
  Yes  No 
    1 102

The reduced kNN model predicts fewer survived outcomes than the full model, and logically more death outcomes. The reduced model is way more likely to classify a patient as a high risk of death. It is strange, though, that the reduced model predicted survival for only 1 patient. Additionally, the full model has higher accuracy in prediction by having the yes and no counts closer to the actual counts in the test set, which were 60 for yes and 43 for no. This model can be used on new data to predict the possible outcome for a patient, given they have data for all the relevant variables.

5.3 Naive Bayes

A Naive Bayes model is created for both the full set of predictors and the reduced set. It is suitable for a binary target variable and also explores predictions based on probability of the target variable. However, it makes an assumption that predictors are independent given the target variable, which should be noted. The model is trained on the training set and applied to the test set.

An important step before running Naive Bayes analysis is to check whether the training set includes any categories for categorical variables which have no observations, as due to the independence assumption of Naive Bayes, the conditional probability formula used by Naive Bayes would result in a value of 0 throughout, if there is a single 0 present. Therefore, the summary of each categorical variable in the training set and the Survived category is examined.

Since for the Ascites variable, there is no case for a patient with Ascites who survived, the conditional probability formula leads to a product with a value of 0 all throughout the naive bayes formula. This means that laplace smoothing needs to be used, which adds a small value to each category to avoid the product being 0 in the conditional probability formula. Given the small number of observations, the laplace value should not distort the values too much, hence the standard value of 1 is used, as it is the smallest possible value.

nb_model_all = naive_bayes(predictors, data = data_train_prep, laplace = 1)

6 Model evaluation

Because the target variable Survived is a binary variable, ROC curves, AUC, and confusion matrices can be used as measures of model performance. As confusion matrices can be used, all models can be held to a standard.

summary(data_true_test)
  Yes  No 
   60  43
60/(60+43)
  [1] 0.5825243

Since the test set includes 60 cases of “Yes” and 43 cases of “No”, this means that if a model always guesses “Yes” it’s accuracy would be around 58%. Therefore all models are expected to at least somewhat improve on this and hence if it has an accuracy of higher than 58%, it has at least some discriminatory ability.

6.1 Evaluation of the Logistic Regression Model

Firstly, the performance of the logistic regression models is evaluated.

# These create a probability vector which we can use for ROC curve and AUC analysis to evaluate the logistic regression model

logreg_all_predict = predict(logreg_all, newdata = data_test_prep, type = "response")


# we need to assign classes for the logistic regression probabilities of the probability vector in order to evaluate the logistic regression model using a confusion matrix

logreg_all_class = factor(ifelse(logreg_all_predict > 0.5, "No", "Yes"),
                        levels = levels(data_test_prep$Survived))
summary(logreg_all_class) # check if the classificaiton is correct
  Yes  No 
   66  37
conf.mat.plot(logreg_all_class, test_set_kNN$Survived) # confusion matrix for the logistic regression for the full set of predictors
  Setting levels: reference = "Yes", case = "No"

# sensitivity

30/(13+30)
  [1] 0.6976744
# specificity

53/(7+53)
  [1] 0.8833333
# accuracy

(53/(7+53) + 30/(13+30))/2
  [1] 0.7905039

Since the research is concerned with predicting which patients require urgent care and hence are likelier to be closer to death, the “No” category for the Survived variable is used as the positive class. This means that the sensitivity of the logistic regression with all predictors is 0.698, specificity is 0.883 and balanced accuracy is 0.791. Although these values are quite high, in practice this means that the model fails to catch almost 3 out of 10 people who are likely to die, which in healthcare can be costly. Comparing to the baseline model, the accuracy is above 58% so they model has discriminatory ability. The balanced accuracy is quite high, combined with a moderate level of sensitivity, this means that the model is useful.

# we create roc curve for the logistic regression model

roc_logreg_all = roc(test_labels, logreg_all_predict)
# this code is to create a graph showcasing the ROC curve and AUC values for the logistic regression model
ggroc(list(roc_logreg_all), size = 0.8) + 
    theme_minimal() + ggtitle("Logistic regression ROC plot with AUC value") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#fbc531"), 
    labels = c(paste("AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_logreg_all), 3))
               )) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.7, .3), text = element_text(size = 17)) +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed")

The AUC value for the logistic regression model using all predictors is .854. The AUC values is close to 1, meaning that the model offers much better predictive powers than a random model. The curve is closer to the top left corner than it is to the diagonal line, evidence for the model having good predictive and discriminative power.

6.2 Evaluation of the Stepwise Regression Model

The step wise regression model is also evaluated.

predict_step_reg = predict(stepwise_model, data_test_prep, type = "response") # we use type "response" as this returns probability values of for the "Yes" category for the target variable Survived in a range between 0 to 1
range(predict_step_reg) 
  [1] 0.01512446 1.00000000
length(predict_step_reg) == nrow(data_test_prep)
  [1] TRUE
# these two lines are to check if the predict function worked as intended on the stepwise regression model
roc_step = roc(data_test_prep$Survived, predict_step_reg) # we create a roc curve for our stepwise regression model by evaluating its performance on the test set
step_class = factor(ifelse(predict_step_reg > 0.5, "No", "Yes"), 
                    levels = levels(data_test_prep$Survived))
summary(step_class)
  Yes  No 
   69  34
conf.mat.plot(step_class, data_test_prep$Survived) 
  Setting levels: reference = "Yes", case = "No"

# sensitivity

29/(29+14)
  [1] 0.6744186
# specificity

55/(5+55)
  [1] 0.9166667
# accuracy

(55/(5+55) + 29/(29+14))/2
  [1] 0.7955426

The sensitivity of the model is .674, the specificity is 0.917, and the balanced accuracy is 0.796. The confusion matrix for the stepwise regression shows that it performs less effectively at predicting the “No” category for the target variable survived, in comparison to the full logistic regression model. This is also displayed by the slightly lower sensitivity value for the stepwise model. Its balanced accuracy is, however, slightly higher relative to the full logistic regression model. It is worth noting that the model still performs better than the baseline model, judging by its accuracy. The stepwise model has higher specificity than the full logistic regression model, but that is not as useful within the scope of the research as sensitivity is.

A ROC curve plot with the Area Under Curve (AUC) values for the stepwise regression model is created and compared to the logistic regression model with all predictors.

# this code is to create a graph showcasing the ROC curve and AUC values for the stepwise regression model and compare it to the logistic regression model using all predictors
ggroc(list(roc_step, roc_logreg_all), size = 0.8) + 
    theme_minimal() + ggtitle("Logistic regression ROC plots with their AUC values") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#353b48"), 
    labels = c(paste("Stepwise regression; AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_step), 3)),
               paste("Logistic regression;   AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_logreg_all), 3)))) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.7, .3), text = element_text(size = 17)) +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed")

The stepwise regression also performs adequately, and it has a similar ROC curve and AUC value when compared to the logistic regression. However, the stepwise regression model does preform slightly better in terms of the AUC value, having a higher value than the full logistic regression model. Both of the models surpass the baseline model and have ROC curves which are closer to the top left corner (ideal) that to the diagonal line (performance of a random model).

6.3 Confusion matrices

Next, the kNN model is evaluated.

prob_naive_bayes_all_pos = prob_naive_bayes_all[, "No"] 
prob_knn_data_all = prob_kNN_all[, "No"] 
prob_naive_bayes_new_pos = prob_naive_bayes_new[, "No"] 
prob_knn_data_new = prob_kNN_new[, "No"] 
# here we create a single vector which shows the probability of the patient surviving for every case in the test set
test_labels = data_test_prep$Survived
# we create ROC curves for both Naive Bayes and kNN models, in both cases for both the full set of predictors and reduced set of predictors. 
roc_nb_all = roc(test_labels, prob_naive_bayes_all_pos)
roc_knn_all = roc(test_labels, prob_knn_data_all)
roc_nb_new = roc(test_labels, prob_naive_bayes_new_pos)
roc_knn_new = roc(test_labels, prob_knn_data_new)
conf.mat.plot(kNN_5_all, test_set_kNN$Survived) # confusion matrix for our kNN algorithm for the full dataset
  Setting levels: reference = "Yes", case = "No"

(52/(8+52) + 21/(22+21))/2

The kNN algorithm actually has a sensitivity of less than 0.5, which is quite poor for the aim of the model. As the model is supposed to spot patients who are likely to die, this model would miss over half of such cases where a patient requires urgent care. It performs only a bit better than the baseline model, with an higher accuracy by approximately 8%. The kNN model does have high specificity, which would be predicting survival for a patient, however, it is debatable how useful that is in context of cirrhosis.

This model is worse than the baseline model based on balanced accuracy. The sensitivity is very high, but the specificity is 0. That is because the model predicted all the the cases to be “No” for the survived variable but 1. The Naive Bayes model with all predictors has a sensitivity of 0.674, suggesting that it can correctly predict 2 out of 3 cases where a patient is dying. This model performs slightly worse than the logistic regression models and the stepwise regression model in terms of sensitivity and accuracy, although it is more accurate than the kNN model. The Naive Bayes model using the reduced set of predictors performs worse overall than the Naive Bayes with the full set of predictors, as its sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy are all lower. Due to the low sensitivity score, this model is not recommended to be used, because that is the most important factor this research is looking at.   theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.7, .3), text = element_text(size = 17)) +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed")

The kNN model using all predictors performs at a mediocre level, but the model with the reduced set of variables performs worse than a random guessing model. That is shown by an AUC value below 0.5 and the ROC curve below the diagonal line. Although this does mean that should the direction be swapped it would perform better, it would still perform worse than the baseline model with an accuracy of 58%. Therefore the kNN model with a reduced set of variables should be scrapped completely.

We will also compare the logistic regression model, Naive Bayes model and the kNN model with each other, for the respective set of predictors.

ggroc(list(roc_logreg_all, roc_knn_all, roc_nb_all), size = 0.8) + 
    theme_minimal() + ggtitle("ROC plots with their AUC values") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#353b48","#0097e6"),
    labels = c(paste("Logreg; AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_logreg_all), 3)),
               paste("kNN;   AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_knn_all), 3)),
               paste("Naive Bayes; AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_nb_all), 3)))) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.7, .3), text = element_text(size = 17)) +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed")

For models using the full set of predictors the Naive Bayes model showcases a significantly stronger predictive power compared to the kNN algorithm. This is shown by the AUC for the Naive Bayes model being 0.855 which is higher than the AUC of the kNN model of 0.727. However, the logistic regression model has an almost identical AUC value as the Naive Bayes model, at 0.854, and its ROC curve is consistently the closest to the top left corner along with the Naive Bayes ROC curve.

ggroc(list(roc_step, roc_knn_new, roc_nb_new), size = 0.8) + 
    theme_minimal() + ggtitle("ROC plots with their AUC values") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#fbc531", "#353b48","#0097e6"), 
    labels = c(paste("Logreg; AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_step), 3)),
               paste("kNN;   AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_knn_new), 3)),
               paste("Naive Bayes; AUC=", round(pROC::auc(roc_nb_new), 3)))) +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank()) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.7, .3), text = element_text(size = 17)) +  
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 1), color = "grey", linetype = "dashed")

For the reduced set of predictors a similar pattern can be seen, as the logistic regression model performs the best with its ROC curve the closest to the top left corner and its AUC value being the highest out of the three models, at 0.867. However, the difference between the Naive Bayes model and the Logistic regression model is small, but the kNN model performs significantly worse throughout, in comparison to the other two models, for both the full and reduced set of predictors. None of the models achieve a near perfect result of identifying correct cases of patient survival, however, the kNN model perfoms particularly poorly in comparison to the other models, in particular the kNN model with the reduced set of predictors, which performs worse than the benchmark. Reducing the number of predictor variables gives a trade off of reduced accuracy (for the reduced models) for model complexity. This may be beneficial when some of the predictor variables are not available for a patient. However, all of the models achieve the purpose of predicting the survival outcome of a patient. The logistic model gives insight into which variables have the most significant impact on survival, and a numerical representation on how they impact the odds of surivial, provided by the coefficients of the regression. Some of the limitations of the models include the fact that the test set had only 103 observations, which is not optimal. Furthermore, the models do not show any causal relationships, only offering predicitve capabilities. For medical research, causal relationships are important, however, the models achieve the main purpose of this research. Additionally, some of the relationships may not be exactly linear, as are most cases in real life, which may cause the regressions to be not at their best accuracy.

7 Communication and Deployment

The logistic model that was created performs consistently better, including across the most important metric for this analysis, the sensitivity. The kNN model does not offer much use because it is the worse performing model overall. The Naive Bayes can be useful for predicting an individual patients risk because it can be applied on new data, given that new patients will have the same medical metrics taken. Furthermore, the Naive Bayes model is a fast, efficient and easy-to-use model in practice and although it is somewhat less accurate than the logistic regression, it still provides a competitive result and has some practical advantages. However, for an interpretative outlook, the logistic regression is best at explaining which variables (at what quantity and direction) increase chances of death for the patient. Looking at the logistic model in more detail, it was found that the model which uses the full set of variables performs better for the key sensitivity metric than the one with reduced variables. The only drawback is a lower specificity value. However, the reduced logistic regression has a higher AUC value. The results for the reduced logistic model are below, including only coefficients significant at an alpha level of 5%, interpret as the increase in chances of death for a 1 unit increase in the variable.

A 1 year increase in age is associated with an increase in odds of death by 5.68%. Age is also significant at a 1% level. A 1 unit increase in bilirubin is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 22.056%. A 1 unit increase in alkaline phosphatase is associated with an increase in odds of death by 0.0245%. A 1 unit increase in SGOT is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 1.0070%. A 1 unit increase in platelets is associated with a decrease in odds of death of a patient by 0.47197%. A 1 unit increase in prothrombin is associated with an increase in odds of death of a patient by 54.2541%.

The final results did not align with the initially hypothesized factors that affect patient mortality, mainly the coefficient for Drug and sex being rather insignificant. The results for copper in blood is not significant at the 5% level. However, the main results align with part of the hypothesis that variables in the Child-Pugh model have a positive relationship with chance of death of a patient, mainly prothrombin. Some practical recommendations that can be made is placing older patients in the high risk category immediately, as a higher age was associated with increased likelihood of death. On the other hand, older patients can be given priority for liver transplants, which goes against the current trends. Additionally, patients who have higher counts of prothrombin in their body also need to be placed into a high risk category, as increased levels contribute to a higher chance of mortality. Furthermore, one of the strongest predictors of death was prothrombin time, or the time it takes for a clot to form. This can outline what blood tests are done for newly diagnosed patients and how patients are classified based on the results. Hence, one of the most important tests that should be conducted is a prothrombin time test, was this was shown to be a strong predictor of death. This result was also significant for both the complete set of predictors, as well as the reduced set of predictors. Given the relatively similar performance of the logistic regression model for both the full set of predictors from the dataset and the reduced set of predictors, in practice it could be more beneficial to use the model with the reduced set of predictors. Although its performance is slightly higher than that of its full set countrepart, according to the AUC value and ROC curve, the performances are similar, and the performance of the model using all predictors comes at a key cost of model complexity, requiring more data and hence more time and resources in patient care and treatment. In real life situations, especially where time in terms of hours or even minutes can be the difference between life and death for a patient, a simpler model could prove more practical, as it requires less tests and hence would be quicker to complete. However, in situations where doctors are not limited by time and resources, the models utilizing the full set of predictors would prove more accurate. The main limitations of the research is that most of the data came from female patients, so it would be useful, as further research, to extend the model, particularly to investigate whether there are differences in classification for female and male patients. It may be that the disease disproportionately affects female patients, but this does not mean that male patients are not just as important to investigate. Some other data that would improve this research, apart from data from more male patients, is non-medical testing data. For example, a patients diet, occupation, etc. This data can be used to create models which predict how likely a patient is to be diagnosed with cirrhosis, or risk factors which can create complications during the illness. The results can be applied to real life in different ways, the Naive Bayes model can be created into a tool which, based on a patients medical metrics, outlines their survival chances. The regression can be incorporated into a similar system but more complex, providing a detailed analysis of why a patient is in the high risk category and what treatment can be done to lower the factors which increase their mortality chance. Some privacy considerations that arise from this research is patient medical information confidentiality, but this can be resolved with saving patient data in the system by non identifiable characteristics. Some practical considerations include the cases where a newly diagnosed patient refuses to undergo certain medical tests, then it would be rather difficult for the model to give an accurate risk classification, however, some blood/urine test measures can be imputed as it was done in this analysis. All in all, multiple models were created which offer predictive power for a cirrhosis patient’s survival status. The most significant metrics which are associated with an increased chance of death are the age of the patient, and counts of alkaline phosphatase, serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase, and prothrombin (as per the full logistic regression model).
